S13v12-1hP1P2:
Your Little Forming Group Already Is the Community

Don't worry about getting land yet. If you've got a small handful of people who want to make a community but aren't sure yet, you are already a community, even if it's still an untested one. It sounds cheesy but it's true.

Don't even think about combining ownership or other big resources until you have gone through at least one real conflict together and really dealt with it. Not 'dealt with it' by writing a vision statement and shaking hands, or by calling a truce nobody believes, like "Let's all just agree to leave each other alone". But really, truly dealt with it. That's the real relational pl/ork of each of you naming what happened, giving each of you time, finding whatever is there (jealousy, humiliation, fear, old material, whatever), and dealing with it until the emotional pressure has changed enough that an agreement actually means something. Until then, what's it worth?

S13v12-3P1: Who has the title to the land? It matters so much! Whoever has it has a massive amount of power over the community. If the deed is in the founder's name, then they're really a landlord just with a philosophy. If three members out of twelve own everything, then there's effectively two classes of members even if the literature says everyone's equal.

S13v12-4P7: If someone will have a role in your group that has serious consequences, involving kids, shared resources, medicine, vehicles or private records, you want to know how they handle that specific thing. I wouldn’t hand someone the van keys just because they’re great with kids! You can find out by asking if you’ve seen them do this thing before, and asking for references if appropriate. Give people access to these things in stages and ensure there’s always some way to appeal decisions about these roles to a separate authority if needed.
S13v12-5P1: A safe community can’t promise to keep everyone. Yes, really. If someone is a serious or general danger, keeps violating essential boundaries, or is just impossible to live with, ejecting them can be the right call. If restorative work with them can work in a reasonable amount of time, that’s cool! But if they are a danger to the community, the community doesn’t have to turn into their treatment program.
